title: Healthcare Errors and Near Misses

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Picture knocking a glass off the counter and catching it an inch above the floor. Nothing broke, but the knock still happened, and next time your hand may be slower. That caught glass is the near miss: the mistake was real, and only a quick catch or plain luck stood between it and damage. The event that already landed and shattered is a different category, and so is a glass that simply wore out on its own.

### Question 2

Someone breaks a leg skiing, so that injury came from skiing. If the cast is then applied too tightly and the foot is damaged, the second injury came from the treatment. Adverse event means tracing the harm back to the care rather than to the illness that brought the person in. Nothing in that trace requires anyone to have broken a rule, and an event with no injury at all does not qualify no matter how alarming it felt.

### Question 3

A sentinel is a guard posted to shout when something dangerous appears. A sentinel event is the loudest alarm a hospital has, meaning someone died or was seriously or permanently hurt by care rather than by their disease. The other three terms name quieter alarms further down the same ladder, sorted by how close the danger came: never reached the person, reached them without hurting them, or was simply a trap sitting there waiting.

### Question 4

Think about leaving the house. Forgetting to lock the door is an omission, because the right action never happened. Locking the neighbor's door by mistake is a commission, because an action did happen, just the wrong one. Every option here has a cause involving something not being checked, so the trick is to ignore the cause and ask only one thing: did a required action go undone, or did a wrong action get carried out?

### Question 5

Smoke detectors are useful precisely because smoke arrives before flames. A near miss is the smoke: the fire has not started, but the faulty wiring is already in the wall. An organization that only investigates after someone is burned throws away every free warning it was given, and there are always far more smoke moments than fires, which is what makes them such a rich source of information.

### Question 6

Draw two circles that partly cross. One holds mistakes; the other holds patients hurt by their care. Many mistakes get caught or turn out to be harmless, so they sit in the mistakes-only crescent. Some patients are hurt by a rare reaction nobody could have predicted, so that sits in the harm-only crescent. The slice where the circles overlap, mistakes that actually injured someone, is the piece safety teams work hardest to shrink.

### Question 7

RCA is watching game film after a loss and asking what actually went wrong and why the breakdown was possible. FMEA is walking the field before the game and asking where things could break so they can be fixed in advance. One faces the past, one faces the future. Neither method exists to decide whose fault something was, which is the fastest way to eliminate the blame-flavored options.

### Question 8

Two separate notebooks are in play. The chart is the story of the patient: what was given, how they responded, who was notified. The incident report is the organization's own maintenance log: what broke in our process so we can repair it. Writing "incident report filed" into the chart blurs a care record into a repair record, and afterward neither notebook does its job cleanly.

### Question 9

Follow the vial. It was pulled incorrectly, which is the error; a person caught it, which is the interception; and it never left the pharmacy, which is why it is a near miss rather than something that reached the patient. The crowded shelf where two look-alike vials sit side by side is a separate finding, the trap that was waiting before anyone stepped in it, and traps and trips get classified under different names.

### Question 10

If two nearly identical bottles keep getting confused, one option is taping a sign to the shelf and hoping every tired person reads it every single time. The other is taking one bottle off the shelf so the mix-up becomes impossible. Signs, emails, and yearly modules all route through a human's attention at the worst possible moment. Changing the shelf itself never gets tired or distracted, which is why that class of fix ranks as strong.

### Question 11

If a town hands out rain gauges and suddenly records twice as much rain, the sky did not change; the counting did. Event reports behave the same way, because when people stop fearing punishment, events that were always happening finally get written down. That is precisely why harm has to be measured separately, through chart review or trigger tools, instead of being inferred from how many reports arrive.

### Question 12

Three different rule-makers appear in this question, and separating them is the whole exercise. Congress writes statute, which is where the confidentiality protection for work shared with a Patient Safety Organization comes from. An accreditor writes standards a hospital agrees to follow to keep its seal of approval, which is where the analysis deadline comes from. Professional ethics says be honest with the patient promptly. Only one option pairs every rule with the rule-maker that actually issued it.
